title: India Rejects China's Objection on Ladakh Names: 'No Denial Can Change This Fact'
excerpt: The MEA restated that Ladakh is an integral part of India after Beijing called the naming of 28 locations, including Gogra and Hot Spring, illegal.
body:
• India has reiterated that Ladakh is an "integral and inalienable part of India," rejecting China's objection to New Delhi's naming exercise in the Union Territory.
  • On October 2, India formally gave standard names to 28 places and geographical features in Ladakh, including the 2020 friction points Gogra and Hot Spring.
  • China's foreign ministry said Beijing has never recognised the Union Territory of Ladakh and called the naming move "illegal and invalid."
  • MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the home ministry's announcement was self-explanatory and aimed at accurate identification of the locations.

India on Tuesday rejected China's objection to the standardisation of place names in Ladakh, restating its position that the Union Territory is an integral part of the country and that Beijing's denial changes nothing.

"It is reiterated that the UT of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India. No amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact," Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, responding to media queries on remarks from Beijing. He added that the home ministry press release behind the exercise was "self-explanatory."

What India announced

On October 2, the government — in consultation with the Ladakh administration — formally identified 28 places and geographical features in the Union Territory under standard names for the official map of the Survey of India, according to reporting by Dainik Jagran and PTI. The list covers peaks, passes, land areas and water bodies, and includes locations of direct military significance along the Line of Actual Control (LAC): Gogra and Hot Spring, both friction points in the 2020 standoff, along with features such as Brangsa, Chapchingal Pass, Kuksel and the Skamri and Parpik glaciers. The stated aims were precise identification on official maps and better public awareness of the sensitive border region.

China's response

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Tuesday that China has never recognised the "so-called Union Territory of Ladakh unilaterally and illegally established by India" and firmly opposed the announcement of standard names. "The move is illegal and invalid and cannot change the fact that the relevant areas in the western sector of the China-India boundary have always belonged to China," she said.

"No amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

Why names on a map matter

Place-name standardisation has become a recurring instrument in the India-China boundary dispute. Beijing has repeatedly issued its own lists of Chinese names for places in Arunachal Pradesh, which India rejects; New Delhi's Ladakh exercise applies the same logic in reverse, embedding Indian administrative naming across a territory whose status China disputes. The locations chosen are not obscure: Gogra and Hot Spring were among the points where Indian and Chinese troops faced off after the standoff that began in May 2020 in the Pangong Lake area and turned deadly in the Galwan Valley. Disengagement at the friction points began in 2022, but the boundary itself remains undemarcated and the political claims unchanged.

What's next

Neither side signalled any change to deployments or dialogue as a result of Tuesday's exchange. The war of words is best read as both capitals putting their positions on the record — India that its cartography is a settled administrative act, China that it does not accept the premise — while the LAC remains quiet but unresolved.
